newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai real estate in slump but soft landing seen.
newsitem.headline: Thai real estate in slump but soft landing seen.

text.p: The depressed Thai real estate market could be in for a soft landing despite declining property values and the possible failure of some heavily geared developers, property consultants and analysts said on Friday.

Real estate rentals and prices could drop by between five and 11 percent this year, but any slump would not be as bad as that felt in some other Asian nations in the past 15 years, said David Simister, managing director of property Richard Ellis.
"In terms of falling values and overall impact I think Bangkok has a good chance of a relatively soft landing," he added.
Hard hit office, house and condominium markets could take up to five years to recover as an oversupply hung over the sector and market fundamentals weakened, they told Reuters.

Modestly healthy demand in most sectors of the market underpinned prices and there were signs that developers recognised the severity of the oversupply situation and were beginning to halt, delay or cancel existing projects, he said.
"There will be some price adjustment, some troubled projects having to offer much more significant discounts, but not an overall downturn," Simister said.
"The other factor that is important is that Bangkok values have not shot up...indeed, prices haven't increased across the board since 1991," he added.
His remarks were supported by consultant Jones Lang Wootton (JLW), which said in a report that demand for city centre office space actually increased through the first quarter.

"The improvement seen in the Bangkok central business district during the first quarter shows that market fundamentals, though weakening, have not collapsed as many have anticipated and there remains continued occupier demand," JLW's director of research Craig Plum said in the report.
Falling values were attracting potential foreign buyers, but transactions so far this year were minimal as Thai developers remained reluctant to sell prime properties, Simister said.
"The reason why we haven't been swamped by Hong Kong and Singaporean buyers buying up the projects of distressed property companies is there is a lack of good stock," he said.
"Their first choice would be to get into the office sector. They may get into other sectors because the Thai property owners are not letting go of the best properties," he added.
Some highly geared Thai developers, facing borrowing costs which at a 13.25 percent minimum are among the highest in Asia, were unlikely to survive the current crisis, he said.

Thai government plans to support the market to limit the damage that property firm failures could inflict on the finance sector were welcome, despite doubts surrounding their workability, Simister said.
To rescue cash-strapped property firms, the authorities last month said they would issue up to 100 billion baht worth of zero-coupon bonds and lend funds raised to those in need.
There were concerns an alternative, or additional, proposal to run a bond-funded rescue through a Property Loan Management Organisation, though welcome, was less workable, he said.
The first issue of the bonds was due next week by the government's Property Loan Management Organisation, which will buy collateralised property loans from financial institutions. ($1 = 26 baht)
